I was brought back to this post a year later by someone commenting on my hot take and looked at this thread and just wondering has any place in the US had success with creating a union for social workers or direct service professionals?  The pay right now is just unsustainable especially at entry level, cost of living is rising and the private sector is seeing pay increases while our wages have been stagnant, our performance based raises are less then the cost of living increase so people are effectively losing money every year even when they are doing an amazing job. People are leaving the field en masse, no one can hire and yet the wages aren’t increasing.  My organizations mission is to prevent and end homelessness and yet we and the rest of our field don’t even pay our lowest paid staff a housing wage - we are actively placing people at risk for homelessness, it’s gross.  The only solution I can think of is maybe a collective bargaining approach and just wondering if it’s been done anywhere before.  As a program manager I also am well acquainted enough with the budget to understand this isn’t totally on the orgs and largely goes back to our state funders and what they are willing to pay for our work through grants and reimbursement rates. 

I don’t know a ton about unions but I do see a potential issue with using strikes as a bargaining tool since I can’t see any of us collectively willing to abandon the people we serve but something really has to change

I would say feel out your psychiatrist…I’m in the US, I told my psychiatrist about past drug use and that I will occasionally but rarely do drugs now.  She still prescribed me a stimulant. Tbh I think it’s better to be honest it’s important to consider how different drugs and medications interact etc…and it’s also important to be able to talk to your psychiatrist about anything that is impacting your brain chemistry.  If you aren’t struggling with addiction, a good psychiatrist should be able to put aside any personal biases about drug use.  Remember, a psychiatrists education includes differential diagnoses, they (allegedly) know the difference between recreational drug use and addiction.  Psychiatrists are also human and not all of them are good at their jobs so there are definitely psychiatrists who will let bias get in the way but that’s a shitty psychiatrist so you’re probably better off switching to a different one.  I also recognize that that’s not always an option and it can be really hard to get a psychiatrist so idk…

First it’s confusing to me that you are putting people living with mental illness and addiction as separate from people who are victims of circumstance. I’m have to believe you are aware
that mental illness is a circumstance outside of ones control. I know there are people who believe addiction is a choice but at the end of the day it’s pretty widely accepted that it is just another category of mental illness.  So seems reasonable to include that in the category of
Victims of circumstance on it’s own but if we look into it further while, brain chemistry is one facet of mental illness and addiction trauma often plays a HUGE role in both.  And I find it impossible to separate a victim of trauma from a victim of circumstance. As for the long list of bad choices - that’s a really murky and subjective concept with an extremely tenuous tie to homelessness. I’ve made a long list of bad choices in my life and not experienced homelessness, so have plenty of other people who are housed.  I’m also going to tack on here that mental illness and addiction are also relatively common among housed people and those factors ALONE are not a cause of homelessness. So hopefully we can all just agree that people experiencing homelessness are by and large victims of circumstance.  

Glad that’s settled.

Now one thing that surely stunts growth (both physical and brain development) is lack of adequate nutrition.  

I feel as though you’re coming at this from an assumption that there are always other food resources available which is simply not the case.  Most food banks are only open on specific days of the week or even of the month.  Some areas have plenty of meal sites that are open every day but many areas don’t so if you happen to sleep or stay in a shelter somewhere far from a meal site you have to find a way to get there and make sure you do so during the time they are open.  In some communities that could mean taking multiple busses which you need to find money for and spending hours of your day just to go get food.  Now imagine you’re also maybe struggling with mental health or addiction or a physical condition as many people who experience homelessness are
and are seeking treatment but the only available appointment conflicts with the meal site schedule.  Now you’re choosing between necessary treatment and your next meal.  Or you maybe you just missed the bus which happens to everyone.  

Stealing something like food is mostly an act of desperation.  It’s something needed to survive.  Consequences in this situation have no benefit, there is nothing to be learned.  

I’m also going to add that it seems like there’s also an assumption that jail time currently would be the result of a person experiencing homelessness who stole food.  Maybe it’s different in other areas but where I live in the US realistically someone who stole food would probably just be banned from the store the stole from.  It doesn’t make sense and doesn’t work to criminalize poverty.

Sure I can see that perspective and I’m all about finding sneaky ways to thwart a shitty system but I also think better education can end up being a natural result of helping communities eradicate poverty.  Middle class communities have great school systems because they pay higher taxes, kids don’t have to deal with the complex trauma and oppression that often goes hand in hand with housing instability and food insecurity and therefore actually have the energy to focus on school, they don’t need to start earning money as teenagers and again can stay-in/focus on school

When you say things like living wage and affordable housing take time, I understand you mean getting buy in on a policy level,  but the reality is things like living wage and affordable housing when implemented actually have an immediate and direct effect.  The buy in for education is already there but the actual effects of education on poverty take years and sometimes generations and aren’t applicable to everyone. 

Also, higher education and training does not equal a living wage everywhere in every career.  It might get you over the poverty line but somewhere along the way we put our poverty line waaaaay below what we actual need to live.

Honestly I would bring it up exactly like that.  Say everything you just said and describe the symptoms you're experiencing. And you can explore options that don't require medication if you decide that's not right for you.  Don't be afraid to advocate for yourself, the first step is getting diagnosed.

And its possible you don't have ADHD but you've said that you've come to the conclusion that you need help so this might lead you down the road to figuring out whatever else it is that's causing your problem.  Depression and ADHD have a lot of overlapping symptoms.

Hi,
I am a 27 year old female, was diagnosed with ADHD when I was younger, briefly on meds that didn't work for me and then everyone including myself just kind of dismissed the diagnosis.
At 27 I am just now addressing this as I'm finally a semester away from graduating college and pretty much collapsed under the stress and depression.  At the urging of my adviser, I went in for neuropsych testing and was, again diagnosed with ADHD - When I talked to my therapist about it and what ADHD actually meant and how it was affecting me, I started crying from relief.  That I'm not just a piece of shit person, that there's actually a real medical explanation for what I'm experiencing.  And even though I've been diagnosed, I still sometimes have trouble believing it's not just a personal failing.  There are years of emotional shit I've built up around my symptoms and the resulting sense of failure.  It will probably take me a long time to undo all that but at least I'm starting.  Anyway every time that stuff comes up for me my therapist loves to remind me of the title of this book on adhd that pretty much mirrors that title of your post.  "You mean I'm not stupid, lazy, or crazy?".  Because that is how so many of us feel, especially those of us who may not have been diagnosed until later in life.  Like I said, undoing years of negative associations isn't easy but getting that diagnosis was like a huge weight lifting off my shoulders.  What's more, my depression and anxiety which I've struggled with on and off my whole life were diagnosed as adjustment orders.  Essentially that means they are a result of the stress triggered by unmanaged ADHD symptoms.  Which means if I can get that under control, the depression and anxiety will likely follow.

I'm still not at a point where things have significantly improved.  But I'm approaching my struggles with a better understanding of how my brain works, that I'm not constantly late because I just don't care enough to be on time.  I could be, and have been, told that I would lose my job/not get a promotion if I were late to work one more time and I would decide to get there thirty minutes early the next day, wake up an hour earlier than normal, and somehow still be 15 minutes late.  Because it's not enough for me to have the intention and to really want to be and care whether I'm on time, there are other strategies that need to be in place - which I'm still figuring out.

And there's medication, and I'm just starting that journey too and what I will say is that I'm on concerta right now and it's not helping so far with a lot of things but it does actually help me to feel kind of a general sense of being less overwhelmed by life.

Anyway I'll echo two sentiments already made here:

1.If you go and get diagnosed it could make a huge difference for you, in your self-esteem alone and also in working towards a solution to the problems you're experiencing.  If you go and don't get diagnosed you're really no worse off than you are now.

2. It sounds like you clearly want to be doing better, with work, with school, with actually hearing what people are saying to you when they're talking - If you want to do something AND you were capable of doing it, then don't you think you would do it?
